blocks.text: Quick verdict

Rayobyte is the better value for most residential scraping: $35 for 10 GB against $80 at Bright Data's list price, about $200 for 100 GB against a $499 minimum plan, $0.90/GB at a terabyte, and traffic that never expires. Bright Data is the better choice for hardened targets, precise ZIP, ASN or carrier targeting, SOCKS5 (Rayobyte's residential gateway lacks it), and managed products such as Web Unlocker and the SERP API. Enterprise compliance needs also favour Bright Data.

Bright Data and Rayobyte both sell residential, datacenter, ISP and mobile proxies, but at very different price points. Bright Data is the premium, enterprise-grade platform with deep targeting and managed unblocking products. Rayobyte is a US-based value provider whose non-expiring residential traffic falls to $0.90/GB at a terabyte. This comparison shows when Bright Data's extra capabilities justify a large price premium and when Rayobyte is the smarter buy.

blocks.text: Bright Data in 2026: what you get

Bright Data, formerly Luminati, is the default enterprise pick for teams that want every collection tool under one contract. Its residential pool is one of the deepest available (150M+ advertised IPs across 195 countries), targeting goes down to city, ZIP and ASN, and the company layers managed products such as Web Unlocker and the Scraping Browser on top. You pay for that breadth: entry pricing is the highest of the major providers unless a promotion is running, and access to some target categories requires a compliance review.

Strengths: Deepest targeting in the market (ZIP, ASN, carrier); Managed unblocking, SERP and browser products under one account; Mature compliance and KYC processes that enterprise buyers ask for; Very large residential pool for high-rotation work. Weak spots: Highest list price per GB at low volume; Dashboard and zone setup take time to learn; Some targets need a compliance review before access.
Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte combines one of the strongest datacenter proxy catalogs with a simple residential offer. Residential traffic is bought in volume bands, from $3.50/GB below 50 GB down to $0.90/GB at a terabyte, and it never expires. Users often praise its human support team. The trade-offs are HTTP-only residential access and limited public data on pool size.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Pricing: Bright Data vs Rayobyte

Bright Data lists residential traffic at $8/GB pay-as-you-go with no commitment, and it frequently runs 50%-off promotions that bring that to about $4/GB. Monthly plans start with the Growth tier at $499 for roughly 141 GB (about $3.50/GB) and fall to around $2.50/GB on the largest public plan.
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $35 with Rayobyte and $80 with Bright Data: a 56% saving in Rayobyte's favour. At 100 GB a month, Rayobyte is the cheaper option at about $200 against $499 for Bright Data, roughly 60% less. Look past the per-GB figure too. Rayobyte lets unused traffic carry forward, while Bright Data's allowance does not (monthly plan allowances reset each cycle). For irregular workloads, that difference can outweigh a small gap in list price.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Rayobyte does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. Bright Data lists '150M+' and Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, Bright Data lists 195 countries and Rayobyte lists Global. On targeting, Bright Data offers country, state, city, ZIP, ASN and carrier, while Rayobyte offers country, region and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. Bright Data supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in Bright Data's favour. On sessions, Bright Data offers rotating per request or sticky sessions you control per zone, and Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available. Both use a backconnect gateway: you point your tool at one host and port, and choose country, city or session behaviour through parameters in the username.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: its pool depth and Web Unlocker handle hardened targets. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires.
SERP and rank tracking: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: it sells a dedicated SERP API alongside raw proxies. How Rayobyte compares: usable, with no dedicated SERP product.

Social media and multi-account management: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With Bright Data: it is powerful but expensive for low-volume account work. With Rayobyte: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools. Run the same small test on both before committing.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: Bright Data wins. The deciding factor for Bright Data: ZIP-level targeting suits local pricing and stock checks. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: city targeting and low prices at volume.
Ad verification and geo-testing: Bright Data. Bright Data has the edge here. Why: carrier and ASN targeting reproduce what real users see. How Rayobyte compares: fewer carrier or ASN controls.
Tight budgets: Rayobyte. Rayobyte has the edge here. Why: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte. How Bright Data compares: its list price is the highest in this comparison.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. Bright Data: Free trial for business accounts, no card required. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Verification and payment rules differ too. Bright Data: Verification required for some sensitive targets. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test Bright Data and Rayobyte before you commit
The quickest way to choose between Bright Data and Rayobyte is a side-by-side test on the sites and countries you actually care about:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (Bright Data: free trial for business accounts, no card required; Rayobyte: check current offer).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, Bright Data comes out ahead in 4, Rayobyte in 1, and 1 is a tie. That makes Bright Data the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: Bright Data is strongest for enterprise data teams with budget for managed tooling, while Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
